en: Half a Day Inside the Wall: Towers, Hui Lanes, and Side Streets
zh: 城墙内半日：钟鼓楼、回坊与小路
ja: 城壁内を半日で：鐘鼓楼・回族街区・路地

p.src: Near the Bell Tower, orientation appears simple: four broad streets run north, east, south and west toward the gates. That cross is useful only as a starting point. A few minutes to the west, the streets between the Drum Tower, Beiyuanmen, Huajue Lane and Xiyangshi narrow; gateways, shops, courtyards and mosques begin to overlap. The best route inside the wall is therefore not a march to the end of one ‘must-see street.’ Fix the South Gate and Bell Tower in mind, then leave room to wander through the northwest quarter. This chapter uses the wall for scale, the two towers as a hinge, and the Hui neighborhood as a place where people still live, worship and work.

p.src: The wall visible today is chiefly Ming in form. It encloses a later core built from the city that contracted at the end of the Tang and was subsequently expanded; it is not Tang Chang'an's outer wall. The official circuit is 13.74 kilometres, so a complete lap is a main activity, not a warm-up before the lanes. From Yongning Gate, look both ways. Inside are roofs, side streets and the axis toward the Bell Tower; outside are the moat, ring road and the modern city continuing beyond them. If the Hui neighborhood follows, walk only enough of the wall to understand the relationship between gate, wall top and main streets. Descend at an access point confirmed open that day. When an exit is uncertain, return the way you came rather than building a closed gate into the plan.

caption.zh: 登上城墙后，先看墙顶宽度、女墙的连续节奏和前方城楼，再决定只走一段还是把全圈当作当天主行程。现代楼群提醒人：城墙仍嵌在日常城市里。
caption.ja: 城壁に上がったら、路面の幅、連なる胸壁、前方の城楼を見て、短い区間にするか一周をその日の主行程にするか決める。背後の現代都市が、城壁が今も日常の街に組み込まれていることを示す。
caption.en: On the wall, first read the width underfoot, the rhythm of the parapets, and the tower ahead; then decide whether to walk one segment or make the full circuit the day's main activity. The modern skyline keeps the wall anchored in the living city.

p.src: The Bell Tower did not begin at today's crossroads. It was built in 1384 near the earlier centre, around present-day Guangji Street. When the early Ming city expanded east and north, the tower was left too far west; in 1582 it was moved to the meeting point of the four main streets. That relocation matters more than the label ‘city-centre landmark.’ It shows Xi'an resetting its centre after expansion, not an unchanged centre surviving from the Tang. Traffic still surrounds the tower. Approach through the signed pedestrian underpass rather than crossing the surface lanes. Entry is optional. Compare the view from several underpass exits: the tower roof shifts against the avenues, revealing why this junction became the chosen centre.

caption.zh: 到钟楼，不要只拍正面。沿四个方向各看一次：方形台基把楼阁抬到车流之上，四条大街由此展开。接近钟楼应走有标识的地下通道。
caption.ja: 鐘楼では正面写真だけで終わらせず、四方向を一度ずつ見る。方形の台座が楼閣を交通の上へ持ち上げ、そこから四本の大通りが伸びる。鐘楼へは案内表示のある地下通路から近づく。
caption.en: Do more than take a frontal photograph at the Bell Tower. Look down each of the four avenues: the square base lifts the tower above the traffic and makes the city cross legible. Use the signed underpass to approach it.

p.src: Completed in 1380, the Drum Tower predates the Bell Tower's first construction by four years and stands a short walk west. Both served urban timekeeping, but folding them into one ‘Bell-and-Drum-Towers attraction’ hides their different jobs in the street. The Bell Tower occupies the four-way junction, with passage on every side of its square base. The Drum Tower has a rectangular base and a north-south arch that leads toward Beiyuanmen. One clarifies the city's cross; the other forms a threshold from broad West Street into narrower lanes. With limited time, there is no need to climb both. Read both exteriors first, then choose one interior according to that day's exhibition, queue and view, leaving the other to be understood from street level.

p.src: The map works at two scales. The left panel places the 13.74-kilometre wall, four Ming gates and Bell Tower cross in one frame, separating a complete circuit from a short southern segment. The right panel moves to walking scale. Its half-day core joins Yongning Gate, the Bell and Drum Towers, the Great Mosque of Huajue Lane and Beiyuanmen. The drawn line is about two kilometres, before wall access, underpasses, courtyard visits and detours are added. Shuyuanmen and the northern Hui-lane loop are optional branches, not compulsory stops. Streets and sites come from a dated open-map extract; the route is this book's editorial plan. Live navigation, open access points and on-site boundaries take precedence.

caption.zh: 左图比较城墙全圈与南墙短段，右图把半日主线和两条可选支线放进街道尺度。路线为行程示意，不替代实时导航、门点开放或现场边界。
caption.ja: 左図は城壁全周と南壁の短い区間を比較し、右図は半日の基本線と二つの任意ルートを街路の縮尺で示す。経路は行程案であり、当日のナビ、門の開放、現地境界を優先する。
caption.en: The left panel compares a full wall circuit with a short southern segment; the right places the half-day core and two optional branches at street scale. This is route logic, not live navigation or a promise of access.

p.src: Many itineraries use ‘Muslim Street’ to mean Beiyuanmen directly north of the Drum Tower. The name works for arranging a meeting but is too narrow for understanding the area. The Hui neighborhood is a network: Beiyuanmen, Huajue Lane, Xiyangshi, Dapiyuan and North Guangji Street, together with several mosques, homes and everyday shops. Visitor commerce is most concentrated on Beiyuanmen, yet one turn can change both the use of the street and its foot traffic. Quiet does not mean ‘more authentic,’ and a busy frontage does not make the whole district a snack market. A small loop reveals more than retracing Beiyuanmen. Parallel streets can relieve a crowded route, but a residential doorway is not a visitor shortcut.

p.src: The Great Mosque of Huajue Lane does not face a grand forecourt. Its entrance is embedded in the street network, and the courtyards unfold only after entering. Official accounts disagree on its foundation. The city's online gazetteer repeats a Tang date of 742; the Lianhu District Gazetteer marks a Tang foundation as requiring verification; the Shaanxi construction gazetteer cites a 1392 record in the Xi'an Prefecture Gazetteer. Rather than treating 742 as settled, look at the surviving arrangement. Four courtyards progress on an east-west axis. Gates, halls, pavilions and platforms use local timber and roof forms, while the prayer hall at the west end is organized for Islamic worship. In the final court, stop at the visitor boundary shown on site.

p.src: Moving from lane to courtyard first changes the walking pace, not merely the architectural style. A raised threshold checks the step; a gate reveals only part of the next court; shade and stone paving draw the eye farther in. The figure brings those spatial cues together. At the real site, do not hurry only toward the deepest building. After each gate, look back at the previous frame and check whether side courts remain in active use. An axis is not a corridor for visitors to charge straight through. Worship, work and visitor areas may sit beside one another within the same compound. Stopping where the on-site signs require often makes the courtyard order easier to understand.

caption.zh: 从街巷到院落：抬高的门槛、层层门框与树荫让步速自然慢下来。这个编辑场景用于观察空间转换，不对应某一处真实门口。
caption.ja: 路地から中庭へ。高い敷居、重なる門、木陰が歩調を変える。空間の移り変わりを見るための場景で、特定の入口を写したものではない。
caption.en: From lane to courtyard: a raised threshold, layered gate and tree shade change the pace. This editorial scene studies the transition rather than documenting a particular entrance.

p.src: The Hui neighborhood is both a historic district and an active religious and residential area. When a lane narrows, move from side-by-side to single file and keep shop doors, house doors and delivery passages clear. A queue must leave exits for neighboring premises. Before photographing architecture, check whether a close face has entered the frame; ask before photographing a vendor, worshipper or resident.

p.src: Inside a mosque, set your phone to silent, do not lean on thresholds, and keep bags away from hall entrances. If prayer begins or staff narrow the visitor boundary, pause or leave. A public street is open to walking; it does not follow that every open doorway is an invitation. The route needs no language of ‘secret discovery’ to be worthwhile.

p.src: For a half-day, follow the core: take a short wall segment at Yongning Gate, walk South Street to the Bell Tower, turn to the Drum Tower, enter the Great Mosque of Huajue Lane, then finish through Beiyuanmen or a parallel lane. Choose at most one tower interior. A full day can add Shuyuanmen in the morning, place a longer wall walk in the cooler part of the day, and use the afternoon for a small Dapiyuan-Xiyangshi-North Guangji loop. Stop for a proper seated meal along the way.

p.src: On 15 August 2026, the wall's official site still listed South Gate as a principal access point with a longer visitor window, but gates, cycle hire, events and temporary controls change. Check tower entry and mosque visitor boundaries separately. Do not place an inflexible reservation immediately after a full circuit.
